subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:Two electric field lines never cross.
text: Give a reason: Two electric field lines never cross.

points.text: At a crossing, the field would have two directions at one point.
The field at a point can only have one direction.

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:Electric field lines meet a conductor at right angles.
text: Give a reason: Electric field lines meet a conductor at right angles.

points.text: A conductor’s surface is an equipotential surface.
A component along the surface would move charges, which doesn’t happen at equilibrium.

text: Give a reason: A person is safe inside a metal car during lightning.

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:A dipole placed in a uniform field does not accelerate.
text: Give a reason: A dipole placed in a uniform field does not accelerate.

points.text: The two charges feel equal and opposite forces.
So the net force is zero, and it only turns.

text: Give a reason: A comb run through dry hair attracts bits of paper.

points.text: The comb is charged by friction, and it induces opposite charges in the near side of the paper.
The attraction on the nearer charges is more than the repulsion on the farther ones.

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:Charging by rubbing does not violate conservation of charge.
text: Give a reason: Charging by rubbing does not violate conservation of charge.

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:A charged conductor loses charge fastest from its sharp points.
text: Give a reason: A charged conductor loses charge fastest from its sharp points.

points.text: Charge density, and so the field, is greatest at a sharp point.

facts: p12-1a:Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the axis of an electri
text: Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the axis of an electric dipole.

points.text: Take charges ±q a distance 2a apart, and a point at distance r from the centre on the axis.
Write the two fields, from +q and from −q, along the axis, each using Coulomb’s law.
Subtract them, as they point in opposite directions, and simplify to E = (1/4πε₀)(2pr)/(r² − a²)².

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:Using Gauss’s theorem, derive the field due to a long straight wire with uniform
text: Using Gauss’s theorem, derive the field due to a long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ.

points.text: Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L around the wire.
Flux through the curved surface is E × 2πrL, and through the flat ends it is zero.
The charge enclosed is λL, so E = λ/(2πε₀r).

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:Using Gauss’s theorem, derive the field due to a uniformly charged thin spherica
text: Using Gauss’s theorem, derive the field due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell at a point outside it, and state its value inside.

points.text: Choose a concentric Gaussian sphere of radius r outside the shell.
By symmetry the flux is E × 4πr².
The charge enclosed is q, so E = q/(4πε₀r²), as if the charge were at the centre.
Inside the shell, no charge is enclosed, so the field is zero.
Conclusion: outside, it falls as 1/r², and inside, it is zero.

facts: p12-1a:A paint shop charges droplets from a spray nozzle and earths the metal panel bei
text:
A paint shop charges droplets from a spray nozzle and earths the metal panel being painted, so the droplets are drawn to it and wrap round its edges.
(i) Why do droplets repel each other as they leave the nozzle? [1]
(ii) Why does paint also reach the back of the panel? [1]
(iii) What would change if the panel were not earthed? [1]

points.text: (i) They carry charges of the same sign, so they repel, which spreads them into a fine mist.
(ii) Field lines curve round to end on the earthed panel, and droplets follow them.
(iii) It would charge up with the same sign as the droplets and start to repel them.

subject: physics
facts: p12-1a:On a dry day, a student who has just walked across a carpet feels a small shock
text:
On a dry day, a student who has just walked across a carpet feels a small shock when touching a metal door handle.
(i) What causes the student to become charged? [1]
(ii) Why is the shock felt at the handle, and not before? [1]
(iii) Why does this happen less often on a humid day? [1]

points.text: (i) Rubbing against the carpet moves electrons between the shoes and the carpet.
(ii) The handle is a conductor, so charge can flow suddenly once the gap is small enough for the field to break it down.
(iii) Moist air conducts a little better, so charge leaks away before it builds up.

text:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A
(1) volume charge density
(2) conservation of charge
(3) a Gaussian surface
(4) electric field at a point
Column B
(a) An imaginary closed surface drawn to apply Gauss’s theorem, usually chosen to match the symmetry of the charge.
(b) The charge per unit volume of a charged body, in C m⁻³.
(c) The force experienced by a small positive test charge placed there, per unit charge.
(d) The total charge of an isolated system stays the same, though charge may move or change form.

points.text: (1) volume charge density goes with (b).
(2) conservation of charge goes with (d).
(3) a Gaussian surface goes with (a).
(4) electric field at a point goes with (c).

p12-1a:the superposition principle for electric forces
text:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A
(1) a point charge
(2) an electric field line
(3) electric flux through a surface
(4) the superposition principle for electric forces
Column B
(a) A curve whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the electric field there.
(b) A charged body whose size is very small compared with the distances involved.
(c) The net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces due to each other charge, each acting as if the others were absent.
(d) The total of E·dA over the surface, a measure of the field lines passing through it.

points.text: (1) a point charge goes with (b).
(2) an electric field line goes with (a).
(3) electric flux through a surface goes with (d).
(4) the superposition principle for electric forces goes with (c).

Column B

(c) The product of one of the two charges and the distance between them, directed from negative to positive.

points.text: (1) the equatorial plane of a dipole goes with (d).

text:

(1) quantisation of charge
(2) surface charge density
(3) relative permittivity
(4) electric charge
Column B
(a) Any charge is a whole-number multiple of the charge on an electron.
(b) The ratio of the permittivity of a medium to that of free space; it has no unit.
(c) The charge per unit area of a charged surface, in C m⁻².
(d) The property of matter that makes it feel a force in an electric field; it is positive or negative.

points.text: (1) quantisation of charge goes with (a).
(2) surface charge density goes with (c).
(3) relative permittivity goes with (b).
(4) electric charge goes with (d).

facts: p12-1b:Find the combined capacitance of capacitors in series and in parallel, and show
text: Find the combined capacitance of capacitors in series and in parallel, and show which is larger for two equal capacitors.

points.text: In series, each carries the same charge and the potentials add.
So 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
In parallel, each has the same potential and the charges add.
So C = C₁ + C₂.
For two equal capacitors these give C/2 and 2C, so parallel is larger.

facts: p12-1b:A camera flash charges a capacitor from a small battery over a few seconds, then
text:
A camera flash charges a capacitor from a small battery over a few seconds, then empties it through the lamp in a fraction of a millisecond.
(i) Why is a capacitor used, rather than the battery directly? [1]
(ii) If the voltage on the capacitor is doubled, how does the energy stored change? [1]
(iii) What happens to the capacitance if a dielectric with a larger constant is used? [1]

points.text: (i) A capacitor can release its stored energy very quickly, giving a large current for a moment.
(ii) It becomes four times as large, as energy depends on V².
(iii) It increases in proportion to the dielectric constant.

(iii) What area of each plate would make the capacitance 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁰ F, with everything else as in (i)?

text: A paint-spray gun gives each droplet a small charge. Situation: Electric potential (definition). Given: work done = 5 mJ, test charge = 20 μC.
